blocks.text: 摘要：Claude 解决了理论物理学中两个悬而未决的问题，二者都涉及黑洞以及对量子引力理论的探索。第一个问题中，它完成了一项物理学家早在 20 多年前就已提出、却始终无人解出的计算。Claude 的结果表明，与黑洞形成相关的突变，即使在时空不再具有确定形状的地方也依然存在。第二个问题中，Claude 求出了用于检验候选量子引力理论的一种技术的最简版本的精确极限。本文先以通俗方式解释这两项发现，再给出更技术性的细节。预印本见此处和此处。

blocks.text: 现代物理学建立在两大框架之上：广义相对论和量子力学。广义相对论描述恒星这类极大的物体，量子力学描述原子这类极小的物体。两者在预测宇宙行为方面都精确得惊人，但在数学上互不相容。找到一种将二者统一起来的理论——“量子引力”——是该领域最大的目标之一。黑洞是天然的试验场，因为它们是少数同时涉及相对论和量子力学的地方——把巨大的质量压缩在极小的空间里。

blocks.text: 全息对偶的基本思想是：这类理论宇宙中的某些可以用两种方式描述——一种是包含引力和时空的完整宇宙，另一种是完全不含引力的量子描述，“写”在宇宙的外边界上。正如真实的全息图把三维图像编码在二维平面上，量子模型用少一个维度的方式编码宇宙的全部信息（例如，一个具有四个空间维度的宇宙，可以由一个三维的量子理论完整描述）。这样一来，物理学家就能把关于引力的难题转化为量子物理问题，而后者有时更容易回答。

blocks.text: Claude 解决的第一个问题，关乎加热这类理论宇宙时会发生什么。在低温下，宇宙中充满粒子气体；超过某一温度，则会形成黑洞。1983 年，Stephen Hawking 和 Don Page 证明这种转变是突变的：它是一种相变，类似于水在 100°C 时突然沸腾。但 Hawking 和 Page 的计算依赖广义相对论，而广义相对论只在宇宙尺度远大于该描述失效的微小尺度时才成立。当理论宇宙缩小到接近那个更小的尺度时，时空失去确定的形状、变得模糊，没有人知道如何在对偶的引力一侧完成计算。不过在量子一侧，同样的情形至少在原则上是可以计算的。

blocks.text: 我们的宇宙不是这样。差异归结为一个称为宇宙学常数的量，它描述空空间的能量。在我们的宇宙中，这个能量是正的，这使得空间膨胀得越来越快。在反德西特时空中，能量是负的，所以一切都被拉回它开始的地方。霍金和佩奇选择这个宇宙进行计算，是因为它加热时的行为：碗把热量留在里面，所以它能保持稳定的温度。

blocks.text: 当粒子之间几乎不发生相互作用时，物理学家只能一步一步地计算它们的行为。他们先从一个粒子完全不发生相互作用的简化理论出发，然后逐项加入修正，每一项都比前一项更精确，也更难计算。物理学家把这些步骤称为圈。2003 年，Aharony 及其同事意识到，相变究竟是霍金和佩奇预言的突变，还是渐变，取决于一个只出现在三圈计算中的数字。计算这个数字涉及成千上万项，也就是所谓的费曼图，数量多到根本无法手算。2005 年，同一团队完成了该理论一个更简单近亲的计算，发现相变是突变的。但 N=4 超杨-米尔斯理论对应的版本规模要大 10 倍以上，始终没能算完。

blocks.text: 作为一种模型，3D 引力比真实情况简单得多，但它仍然允许黑洞存在，也保留了许多同样的谜团。它为研究时空历史求和提供了一个有用的实验室，也是检验“时空并非宇宙的基本成分，而是从更深层的东西中涌现出来”这一想法的好地方。在广义相对论中，黑洞看起来是光滑的。但在量子引力中，如果放大到最小尺度——普朗克长度，约 10-35 米，在这个尺度上，引力受到的量子效应已无法忽视——黑洞是由数量极其庞大的微小个体构件组成的。物理学家相信，我们所在的四维宇宙也是如此，但三维版本用全息对偶来分析要容易得多。

blocks.text: Summary: Claude has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity. In the first, it completed a calculation that physicists set up more than 20 years ago, but which had never been solved. Claude’s result showed that a sudden transition associated with the formation of black holes persists even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In the second, Claude found the exact limit of the simplest version of a technique used to test candidate theories of quantum gravity. This post explains both findings, first in plain terms and then in more technical detail. The preprints are available here and here.
Introduction

inlines.text: Introduction

blocks.text: Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

blocks.text: The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

blocks.text: The first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page showed that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

blocks.text: In 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. blocks.text: This approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein showed that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.

blocks.text: At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. blocks.text: When particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.

But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10-35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.

For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

blocks.text: Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.

blocks.text: If we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). blocks.text: The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?

blocks.text: This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.

blocks.text: Over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.

blocks.text: Claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve. Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.

It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. inlines.text: Conclusion

blocks.text: These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a new idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.
